Some of this ended up in the appendices for The Return of the King , and it's this that Prime Video has used as the foundation for its TV series. One of the first projects that immediately comes to mind is Reacher , the action series starring Alan Ritchson that has become a flagship property for the streamer in the last four years. One aspect of Reacher that’s certainly appealing for Prime Video is that the streamer can continue investing in the show to return for future seasons without needing to spend hundreds of millions of dollars, a trait it does not share with Prime Video’s most popular fantasy series. We’re talking, of course, about The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power , which returned just two weeks ago for its third season.

items.title: Chemicals, Covid and cabbage: why 2026 has been an amazing year for documentaries
items.summary:
With Musk, NAZA and You Can See Everything finding large audiences, non-fiction cinema is poised to break through. But there are plenty more gripping stories waiting for their turn in the spotlight

There comes a time in the life of every film enthusiast when they must set aside foolish fictions and face up to some hard truths. Specifically, that time arrives each November in the form of the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA for short), with its tales of crisis and strife, angry resistance and everyday human kindness. The world’s largest documentary festival plays out in the city’s twinkling downtown district, quite near the torture museum, and provides a sharp corrective to the confected dramas and A-list pageantry of Cannes, Toronto and Venice. The forecast is bracing, stormy, and occasionally chilling. Hours of darkness; no stars.

We might not wish to live in the world IDFA shows us, but unfortunately we do, and so it pays to stay informed, be engaged. This year’s lineup of 250-plus documentaries steers us around the geopolitical hot spots, from tales of forced displacement in the West Bank to the rolling hell of Gaza; from a jungle-based guerrilla army in Myanmar (in White Tiger Column, the event’s opening night film) through to the traumatised children of the Vietnamese boat people (Carol Nguyen’s superb Still Night, Burning House). Some of these films could have been torn from the headlines. Others, like Raluca Lupascu’s gripping kitchen-sink tragedy A Modern Roma Fairytale, contain…

items.title: ‘Reminds me of home’: why Coming to America is my feelgood movie
items.summary:
The latest in our series of writers picking their most rewatched comfort films is an ode to Eddie Murphy’s beloved culture-clash comedy

“Good morning, my neighbors!” A young Eddie Murphy shouts from the balcony of a shady apartment building. In the bustling Queens neighborhood, he sticks out like a sore thumb with his foreign accent, tailored blazing jacket and red tie. “Hey, fuck you!” A voice yells from below and Murphy repeats the phrase, believing that it’s a greeting rather than an insult. It’s one of the standout scenes from the film Coming to America, because it’s so absurd but effective in that there is a cultural clash going on here.

In Coming to America, Prince Akeem, played by Eddie Murphy, is the sole heir to the throne of Zamunda, a fictitious African country. Instead of having an arranged marriage, Prince Akeem exercises his autonomy and intends to find his own bride somewhere far away from the continent, much to his parents’ chagrin. With the coin-flip and a roll of the personal globe, Akeem and his sidekick Semmi go to America but more specifically Queens because where else would be more fitting to find his bride? While trying to assimilate to the fast pace of New York living, he pursues Lisa, the heiress to a different kind of throne – that of a fast-food business called McDowell’s. The problem is, she’s already engaged to another. Akeem hides his identity as a royal prince and works at her father’s fast-food restaurant to get closer to her. Will Akeem and Lisa fall in love as he cosplays being working class. Will Lisa leave her rich but…
items.t: ‘Reminds me of home’: why Coming to America is my feelgood movie

items.title: Who Is Still Alive review – grief-stricken stories of the places and people lost in Gaza
items.summary:
Nicolas Wadimoff invites refugees to draw a floor plan of their former neighbourhood, bringing raw and agonising pain to the surface

A sombre documentary from the Swiss musician and film-maker Nicolas Wadimoff, who returns to his longstanding interest in Gaza. In this film, a group of survivor-refugees who made it out of Gaza and into Egypt during the bombing gather in an enclosed studio and are invited to draw out a kind of floor plan of what they remember of their neighbourhood. First, this is on paper and then on the studio floor itself; they use that as a basis for their memories of what and who they have lost. (The people who have died are described as having been “martyred”.)

The result is almost unbearably painful. The raw and agonising grief, which perhaps stays just at the waterline of consciousness most of the time, is here brought above the surface. They are people suffering from trauma, carrying videos on their phones of their lost loved ones. One interviewee talks of attending the Edward Said conservatory, now rubble; another talks of her work in film-making and animation. Another man plays poignantly beautiful music on his qanun, a type of zither, and then specifies the point in the music at which he was showered with glass from an explosion while he was playing it in Gaza.

Continue reading...
items.t: Who Is Still Alive review – grief-stricken stories of the places and people lost in Gaza

items.title: The Boy and the Suit of Lights review – a sensitive portrait of an aspiring toreador in a changing Spain
items.summary:
Encouraged by his grandfather and single mother, the teen Borja dreams of a career that will end his family’s poverty, but the protesters are gathering strength

Where last year’s bullfighting documentary Afternoons of Solitude by Albert Serra was a tightly trussed formalistic affair concerned by the question of style in the arena and in art, this Scottish-produced film is a looser, more social-realist approach to la corrida. Swerving a portrayal of the butchery itself, it focuses on the wider community significance of this tradition in the eastern Spanish city of Castellón, via the figure of aspiring teen toreador Borja.

Supported by his harried, cigarillo-smoking single mother, Raquel, Borja hopes that wearing the sequined “suit of lights” will help lift his family out of poverty. Everything in his vicinity seems to point in the direction of the bullring: the Playmobil corrida he stages with his little brother, Erik, the mechanical rodeo bulls they ride at the fairground, the lessons in handling the muleta – the red cloth – he gets from grandfather, Matias, whose own bullfighting ambitions were scotched at an early age. But, as the protesters piling into the arena one day highlight, the bell may already be tolling for the kid’s chosen profession.

items.title: You Can See Everything’s vibes-check approach is an insult to objective truth
items.summary:
For three hours, Nathan Fielder opts not to quiz convicted criminal Elizabeth Holmes on the details of her deception. Instead, he looks into her eyes and asks if she’s for real. Is that why his film has been so successful?

• This article does not contain major spoilers

Sometimes, people who have lied lie about whether or not they’ve lied. They even, on occasion, fail to tell the truth despite having sworn to do so – in court, for instance, or staring deeply into the eyes of someone who is sitting right there.

Is that a shock? Probably not. We all engage in versions of such behaviour every day. We understand that the current climate of mutually clueless echo chambers helps claptrap gain traction. But we can still recognise the difference between little white lies and big red flags. We know that the moment anyone starts using the phrase “my truth” it’s time to cancel the wedding.

Continue reading...
items.t: You Can See Everything’s vibes-check approach is an insult to objective truth

items.title: Delays mean Robert Pattinson doesn’t have to do a third Batman movie. DC Studios had better persuade him – and fast

Can one actor play both Batman and James Bond? This is the question many have been asking since Robert Pattinson was announced as the new 007. The obvious answer is yes: the 40-year-old Englishman has the poise, charisma and steel to join His Majesty’s Secret Service, and saving Gotham could soon become something he fits in between assignments.

Among all the furore over Pattinson’s appointment, it would have been easy to miss some rather less cheering news for the citizens of Gotham. According to the Wrap, delays to The Batman: Part II have freed the actor from his contractual obligation to make a third film. The sequel is now due in February 2028, almost six years after the first instalment. He could still sign a new deal, of course, but Warner Bros will have to persuade its caped crusader to stick around.

items.title: Now get out of that! How can the new James Bond film get around 007’s death in No Time to Die?
items.summary:
Was it all a dream? Has Bond been in hiding? Or will Robert Pattinson simply report to HR on his first day? Russell T Davies, David Hare and more give their takes

“James Bond will return,” says the closing title on No Time to Die, the most recent James Bond film and the final one to star Daniel Craig. It is just as well: Bond has to all appearances been vaporised by sea-launched missiles, having been infected by nanobots programmed to attack his nearest and dearest at the slightest touch. No one would believe that one of the world’s most successful film series would come to such an abrupt halt, but no doubt a little reassurance helped.

Nevertheless, the first order of business for scriptwriter Steven Knight and director Denis Villeneuve will be dealing with it: how to revive and re-energise a character at the heart of the action. Speculation on their best way forward has been rife, and previous examples are not hard to find. Sherlock Holmes was killed off by Arthur Conan Doyle by fighting his arch enemy Professor Moriarty at the Reichenbach Falls in the story The Final Problem, only to resuscitate him a decade later with The Adventure of the Empty House. Superman is apparently killed at the end of Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice, but resurrected in Justice League for the fight against Steppenwolf. Arguably the most enduring pop-culture return is Bobby Ewing’s famous shower scene in the TV show Dallas in 1986, which attempted to ensure continuity by suggesting Ewing’s death was his wife’s dream. And even Ian Fleming toyed with killing off Bond, with a…
items.t: Now get out of that! How can the new James Bond film get around 007’s death in No Time to Die?
